served.stem: A person at rest who breathes rapidly and deeply for several minutes will most likely develop which acid base disturbance?
choices: Metabolic alkalosis from a loss of hydrogen ions
served.bankWhy: Two questions sort every acid base problem: which way did pH move, and what moved it. Blowing off carbon dioxide pulls the carbonic acid equilibrium backward, consumes hydrogen ions, and raises blood pH, and because ventilation caused it the label is respiratory. The choice reading respiratory alkalosis is the fit, and holding your breath gives you the mirror image, respiratory acidosis.

choiceTexts: Metabolic alkalosis from a loss of hydrogen ions

answer.line: Fast, deep breathing blows off CO2. Less CO2 means less H+, so pH rises, and the lungs did it.

steps: Follow the CO2. Rapid, deep breathing at rest blows it off faster than the body makes it.
Less CO2 pulls the carbonic acid equilibrium to the left. That uses up H+, so pH rises: alkalosis.
Ask what moved it. The lungs did, so the label is respiratory.

choices.note: Metabolic acidosis, from ketones or lactic acid, drives fast breathing as the fix. Here the breathing came first and caused the change.
That is hypoventilation: CO2 builds up, H+ rises and pH falls. Blowing CO2 off runs the other way.

choices.text: Metabolic alkalosis from a loss of hydrogen ions
choices.note: Alkalosis holds. But H+ lost from the gut, as in vomiting, is metabolic, and here CO2 left through the lungs.
Breathing is a fast pH lever: change how much CO2 you exhale and blood pH moves within minutes.
Ventilation moved pH up: respiratory alkalosis.

student.lockIt: Ask which way pH moved and what moved it. Lungs moving CO2 means respiratory.
student.hook: Hold your breath: acidosis. Overbreathe: alkalosis.
